newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers turn screw as new talks start.
newsitem.headline: French truckers turn screw as new talks start.

text.p: French unions urged truckers to continue a six-day-old blockade of about 30 towns on Saturday as employers launched a new round of talks in a marathon attempt to lift the pressure on the national economy.

Haulage bosses and unions met at 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) for a third session in as many days, broke off almost immediately when haulage bosses demanded a pause to clarify how widely the talks should range, and resumed talks at 4.30 p.m. (1530 GMT).

The companies have agreed to allow truckers to retire at 55 instead of 60, but they want the state to foot the bill. Unions say talks are stuck over the issues of working hours and payment for all working hours, including time spent loading.

"I'm tempted to ask drivers to tighten the screws a bit more. Now we've got mates who have blocked Rungis (Paris's wholesale food market) and I hope that will continue," the Force Ouvriere union's Roger Poletti told France-Info radio.

Haunted by memories of a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago which badly dented his popularity, Prime Minister Alain Juppe has called on both sides to end the dispute quickly and agreed that a Transport Ministry official chair the talks.

North of the south-western city of Bordeaux, where Juppe is mayor and singled out for the worst protests, truckers lifted a blockade on the A10 highway overnight after earlier letting dozens of exhausted Spanish, Portuguese, German and British colleagues through.
But elsewhere there was no sign of a let-up. Since Friday evening, truckers have virtually blocked a highway to Rungis market south of Paris. Police said produce was getting through.

Tens of thousands of trucks blocked main roads and a dozen fuel depots. The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations ran out of fuel in areas of Normandy and in Bordeaux.
Unions say they would blockade Paris only as a last resort.
"Everything has yet to be negotiated -- working hours and wages are the biggest issues. The bosses have offered nothing," Joel Lecocq of the CFDT union told reporters before the talks.
Unions said the government had agreed to finance early retirement for truckers but only on condition the talks succeed on all other sticking points.

Thousands of foreign truck drivers, mostly British and Spanish forced to drive through France between northern and southern Europe, were stranded in the roadblocks, sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.

The London Foreign Office ordered consulates in France to help stranded British drivers with money and contacts with home. The Spanish embassy advised drivers to lodge complaints with police to claim compensation for rotting cargoes.
More than 1,000 British truck drivers were stuck in blockades across France and British freight operators said the dispute was ruining them.
"We are very concerned at the situation and nothing seems to be happening despite our urgent pleas to UK, French and European authorities," said the Freight Transport Association.
In France, the Association of Food Industry said the protest was starting to weigh on the industry's logistics.
Opposition Socialist leader sided with the truckers, who say they are underpaid and overworked due to cut-throat competition between companies.
"Men cannot accept working 70 hours a week, being forced to drive 15 or 17 hours a day, and seeing the extremely tough and tiring nature of their work go unrecognised," he said.
